title: Optimistic UI — Instant Feedback Before Server Confirmation

subChunks.title: Optimistic UI — Instant Feedback Before Server Confirmation
subChunks.hookHtml: When a user clicks 'Like' and has to wait 500ms for the count to update, the app feels slow. Optimistic UI updates the UI immediately as if the request already succeeded, then corrects it if the server responds with an error. It's the technique behind the instant-feeling interactions in every major social app — and it's straightforward to implement in React.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The optimistic update pattern

  1. User performs an action
  2. Update UI immediately (optimistically)
  3. Send the request to the server in the background
  4. If success: leave the UI as-is (or sync with server response)
  5. If failure: roll back the UI to the previous state and show an error
function LikeButton({ post }) {
  const [liked, setLiked] = useState(post.liked);
  const [likeCount, setLikeCount] = useState(post.likeCount);

  async function handleLike() {
    // 1. Capture current state for rollback:
    const prevLiked = liked;
    const prevCount = likeCount;

    // 2. Update optimistically:
    setLiked(!liked);
    setLikeCount(liked ? likeCount - 1 : likeCount + 1);

    // 3. Send to server:
    try {
      await toggleLike(post.id);
    } catch (err) {
      // 4. Roll back on failure:
      setLiked(prevLiked);
      setLikeCount(prevCount);
      alert('Failed to update like. Please try again.');
    }
  }

  return (
    <button onClick={handleLike}>
      {liked ? '❤️' : '🤍'} {likeCount}
    </button>
  );
}

List-level optimistic updates

function QuestList() {
  const [quests, setQuests] = useState(INITIAL_QUESTS);

  async function handleComplete(id) {
    // Capture for rollback:
    const prev = quests;

    // Optimistic update:
    setQuests(qs => qs.map(q => q.id === id ? { ...q, done: true } : q));

    try {
      await markQuestComplete(id);
    } catch {
      setQuests(prev); // Roll back
    }
  }
}

Optimistic deletion

async function handleDelete(id) {
  const prev = items;
  setItems(items.filter(item => item.id !== id)); // Remove immediately

  try {
    await deleteItem(id);
  } catch {
    setItems(prev); // Re-add if failed
  }
}

Vex: "The key discipline: always save the previous state before mutating. A single line: const prev = items;. The rollback is then one line: setItems(prev). If you forget to save before, you've lost the ability to undo."

When optimistic updates are appropriate

  • Actions that succeed >99% of the time (likes, toggles, reorders)
  • Actions where the delay is perceptible and frustrating
  • When the rollback doesn't cause confusion (toggling a like vs. a payment)

Do not use optimistic updates for destructive or financial operations — where showing a failure is less confusing than a sudden reversal.

storyBeats.text: An apprentice marks a quest as complete. In the old system, the scroll stays blank until the guild's ledger updates — three seconds of nothing. In Vex's system, the quest is marked instantly. The ledger catches up in the background.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: The three disciplines: save the old state before changing it, update immediately, send to the server. If the server rejects the change, one line restores the old state. If it accepts, nothing more is needed. The user never waits.

storyBeats.speaker: Save → update → rollback

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a <TodoListOptimistic />:

  • State: array of { id, text, done } items
  • Each item has a 'Complete' button that marks it done optimistically
  • The async markDone(id) has a 20% chance of failure (simulate with Math.random() < 0.2)
  • On failure, roll back the done state and show <p data-testid="error">Failed</p>
  • Completed items get className="done" and data-testid="done-{id}"

guidedPracticeTests.label: Clicking Complete shows done state immediately

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a <MessageBoard /> from scratch. Users can post messages and delete them. Post and delete use optimistic updates with rollback. Simulate a 30% failure rate for both operations. Show a dismissible error banner when either fails. No scaffold.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the optimistic update pattern to a developer who currently waits for server confirmation before updating the UI. Walk through the three steps, why saving the previous state is critical, and give an example of a use case where optimistic updates are inappropriate.

questions.prompt: What is an optimistic UI update?
options: Updating the UI immediately as if the server request succeeded, then rolling back if it fails
Updating the UI only after the server confirms success
Showing a loading state while the server processes the request
Caching the UI state to avoid refetching from the server
questions.answer: Updating the UI immediately as if the server request succeeded, then rolling back if it fails
questions.explanation: Optimistic updates improve perceived performance by applying changes to the UI immediately. The server request happens in the background. If it fails, the UI reverts to the previous state. If it succeeds, no further UI changes are needed.

questions.prompt: What is the most critical step to include before making an optimistic update?
options: Save the current state in a variable before updating it — needed to roll back if the request fails
Disable the button to prevent double-clicks
Show a loading spinner to indicate the request is in progress
questions.answer: Save the current state in a variable before updating it — needed to roll back if the request fails
questions.explanation: const prev = state; before the optimistic update. If the server call fails, you restore: setState(prev). Without this save, you've lost the ability to undo the optimistic change.

questions.prompt: For which of these actions is an optimistic update INAPPROPRIATE?
options: Completing a payment — the reversal would be confusing and the user needs server confirmation before assuming success
Toggling a like on a social post
Reordering items in a drag-and-drop list
questions.answer: Completing a payment — the reversal would be confusing and the user needs server confirmation before assuming success
questions.explanation: Optimistic updates work for reversible, low-stakes actions that succeed almost always. A payment reversal — showing 'Payment successful' then changing it to 'Failed' — is far more confusing and potentially harmful than the slight delay of waiting for confirmation. Financial operations, account changes, and destructive actions should wait for server confirmation.
